title: Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation for Agentic Knowledge Graph Question Answering

paper.title: Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation for Agentic Knowledge Graph Question Answering
paper.abstract: Abstract Agentic knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) requires large language models (LLMs) to solve complex questions through multi-turn interactions with a knowledge graph (KG). Outcome-supervised reinforcement learning derives verifiable outcome rewards from final answers but uniformly assigns each rollout’s outcome-level advantage to all policy-generated tokens, creating a trajectory-to-operation mismatch since KG operations within a rollout can have varying effects on the search process and final answer. To address this, we propose Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation (OACR), which employs a training-only KG-state outcome model to estimate outcome-reward changes between adjacent KG search states and converts them into operation credit, from which token-wise weights are derived. These multiplicative weights reallocate token-level update magnitudes while preserving the sign of the outcome-level advantage at every generated token. Across three benchmarks, OACR achieves stronger overall performance than existing KGQA methods while using fewer inference-time LLM calls and tokens.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Trajectory-to-operation mismatch under outcome-supervised RL. Left: Successful rollouts may contain non-progressive entity-return operations, while failed rollouts may contain progressive ones. Right: Distribution of progressive and non-progressive entity-return operations across successful and failed rollouts, based on 5,000 such operations generated by Qwen2.5-3B on CWQ. Knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) seeks to answer natural language questions by reasoning over facts represented as directed triples in a knowledge graph (KG) ( Ma et al., 2025 ; Nguyen et al., 2025 ; Tian et al., 2025 ) . Complex KGQA often requires multi-hop reasoning: a model must select relation paths that reach answer entities, follow the correct directions, and avoid irrelevant branches ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Ao et al., 2025 ) . Recent agentic methods based on large language models (LLMs) formulate KGQA as multi-turn interaction with a KG environment ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2024 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Yan et al., 2026 ) . At each turn, the agent issues a schema-valid KG operation, receives a structured observation containing returned relations or entities, and appends both to the accumulated KG search state. This interaction process is well suited to outcome-supervised reinforcement learning (RL): final answers provide verifiable outcome rewards, whereas labels that directly assess the utility of individual KG operations are costly to obtain and usually unavailable during training. We label an entity-return operation as progressive if it reduces the minimum shortest-path distance between the accumulated entity set and the gold answer set, and non-progressive otherwise. Retrieving additional gold answers or verifying constraints may leave this distance unchanged. Figure 2: Training-process diagnostics of outcome-only GRPO in agentic KGQA. (a) Final-answer quality. (b) Raw and smoothed trajectory-to-operation mismatch rates. (c) Rates of rollouts containing both progressive and non-progressive entity-return operations and of non-progressive operations following the first progressive one. (d) Average numbers of all KG operations and entity-return operations per rollout. Motivation. Figure 1 summarizes 5,000 entity-return operations from rollouts generated on ComplexWebQuestions (CWQ) ( Talmor and Berant, 2018 ) by a Qwen2.5-3B model trained with outcome-only Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . In successful rollouts, 65.8% of entity-return operations are non-progressive, while 25.3% in failed rollouts are progressive. Thus, rollout outcome cannot determine whether individual entity-return operations advance KG search. Nevertheless, outcome-supervised RL assigns the same outcome-level advantage to all policy-generated tokens in a rollout, including those serializing progressive and non-progressive operations. We call this mismatch between rollout-level supervision and individual KG-operation effects trajectory-to-operation mismatch . We further examine whether outcome-only GRPO reduces this mismatch. Figure 2 reports the training-process diagnostics. Panel (a) shows both F1 and Hit@1 rising during training, whereas Panel (b) shows the mismatch rate fluctuating between 33% and 36%. Here, a mismatch is a non-progressive entity-return operation in a successful rollout or a progressive operation in a failed rollout. Panel (c) shows that the rate of rollouts containing both progressive and non-progressive entity-return operations remains at 36% to 40%, while the rate of non-progressive entity-return operations after the first progressive operation fluctuates between 42% and 68% and increases toward the end of training. Panel (d) shows that the average interaction length remains stable at 2.9 KG operations and 1.45 entity-return operations per rollout. Together, Figures 1 and 2 show that outcome-only GRPO improves final-answer performance, yet the trajectory-to-operation mismatch persists throughout training and is not explained by changes in KG interaction length. These observations necessitate a credit-assignment method that distinguishes KG operations within a rollout while preserving the sign of outcome-level advantage. A common alternative uses Process Reward Models (PRMs) to score intermediate steps ( Lightman et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) . However, an operation’s effect on the outcome reward depends on subsequent operations and final-answer generation, so treating these scores as independent local rewards or additive local advantages can adversely change the sign of the token-level advantage. Our Work. We propose Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation (OACR) for outcome-supervised agentic KGQA. OACR computes an outcome-level advantage from the rewards of rollouts sampled for the same question and incorporates a KG-state outcome model to estimate outcome-reward changes between adjacent KG search states. It converts these changes into operation credit, assigning larger weights to tokens that serialize KG operations assigned greater credit. The token weights are normalized over all policy-generated tokens in the rollout and remain positive. Multiplying these positive weights by the outcome-level advantage reallocates its magnitude across policy-generated tokens while preserving its sign. The KG-state outcome model is used only during training and introduces no additional inference-time cost. Across three benchmarks, OACR outperforms existing KGQA methods overall while using fewer inference-time LLM calls and tokens. Our main contributions are as follows. • We identify and empirically analyze trajectory-to-operation mismatch under outcome-supervised RL for agentic KGQA: the final-answer outcome does not distinguish whether individual KG operations advance KG search, yet all policy-generated tokens within a rollout receive the same outcome-level advantage. This mismatch persists throughout training. • We propose OACR, which converts estimated outcome-reward changes between adjacent KG search states into operation credit used to construct token weights, thereby reallocating token-level update magnitudes while preserving the sign of the outcome-level advantage. Our code is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/OACR/.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Further discussion of these related methods is provided in Appendix A . LLM-based KGQA. LLM-based KGQA formulates reasoning as explicit KG search, enabling LLMs to construct or revise search decisions for retrieving KG facts ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Long et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . These methods improve KGQA through inference-time search, constrained decoding, or supervised trajectories, orthogonal to our OACR that optimizes a multi-turn KG interaction policy from sampled rollouts. RL for agentic KGQA. Recent work trains KGQA agents from sampled rollouts using outcome rewards or reinforcement fine-tuning to optimize multi-turn KG interaction policies ( Song et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2026 ) . Other studies refine outcome supervision through reward modeling, rejection sampling, or curriculum RL ( Yan et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026b ) . These methods assign rewards to complete rollouts or paths, providing limited distinction among KG operations within a rollout and leaving the trajectory-to-operation mismatch unresolved. In contrast, OACR converts estimated outcome-reward changes into operation credit for constructing token weights across KG operations. Process rewards and credit assignment. Prior work assigns rewards or advantages to intermediate reasoning steps or interaction turns, while preference-based optimization reweights training examples, text segments, or tokens ( Lightman et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ; Zeng et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Rezaei et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Zeng et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . In KGQA, related approaches use step-wise rewards, process reward models, or KG schema information to guide logical-form construction and KG reasoning ( Xiong et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Chen et al., 2026a ) . These methods provide intermediate supervision, search guidance, or optimization weights. However, accumulated intermediate rewards or advantages can change the sign of the token-level advantage. In contrast, our OACR derives weights from outcome-reward changes between adjacent KG search states and preserves the sign of the outcome-level advantage. Figure 3: Overview of OACR. Supervised fine-tuning initializes a KGQA agent, followed by outcome-supervised reinforcement learning with outcome-anchored credit reallocation. The KG-state outcome model is updated using recent OACR rollouts every U U RL iterations and held fixed during each policy update. The entire process is outlined in Algorithm 2 of Appendix F .

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: Figure 3 presents the two-stage OACR pipeline. Stage 1 uses supervised fine-tuning to initialize the KGQA policy. In Stage 2, the current policy samples rollout groups and computes an outcome-level advantage for each rollout. The KG-state outcome model is initially trained on outcome-only GRPO rollouts and periodically updated using recent OACR rollouts. Its estimates for adjacent KG search states are used to compute operation credit and construct token weights. These weights rescale the outcome-level advantage across policy-generated tokens while preserving its sign. Detailed inference rollouts are provided in Appendix I .

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: Training-free baselines include direct prompting with Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and GPT-5, as well as inference-time KG search and planning methods ToG ( Sun et al., 2024 ) , PoG ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , ReknoS ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , and MCTS-KBQA ( Xiong et al., 2025 ) . Training-based baselines use SFT or RL for KGQA and include KG-R1 ( Song et al., 2025 ) , RoG ( Luo et al., 2024 ) , KBQA-o1 ( Luo et al., 2025 ) , Graph-RFT ( Song et al., 2026 ) , KnowCoder-A1 ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , EoG ( Yan et al., 2026 ) , DPRM ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , and SCPRM ( Chen et al., 2026a ) . OACR SFT denotes the SFT-initialized policy. OACR GRPO further optimizes this policy using outcome-only GRPO, while OACR additionally applies outcome-anchored credit reallocation.

sections.heading: Main Results.
sections.text: OACR improves both F1 and Hit@1 over OACR SFT across all three datasets and backbones (Table 1 ; split-wise GrailQA results are provided in Appendix K ). It also outperforms OACR GRPO in both metrics on all three datasets with Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-7B. The largest F1 gains over OACR GRPO occur on CWQ, reaching 2.9 and 4.6 points for the two backbones, respectively. Among reported methods using the same backbone, OACR with Qwen2.5-3B outperforms KG-R1 in Hit@1 on CWQ and WebQSP. On these two datasets, OACR with Qwen2.5-7B ranks first in both metrics, while OACR with Llama-3.1-8B ranks first in F1 and second in Hit@1. With these two backbones, OACR ranks second to EoG in both metrics on GrailQA. The gains over OACR GRPO support OACR’s use of estimated outcome-reward changes to construct multiplicative token weights that reallocate the outcome-level advantage across KG operations, improving final-answer quality beyond outcome-only GRPO.

sections.heading: Ablation Study.
sections.text: Using absolute KG-state outcome estimates ( Absolute state est. ) or removing the temporal ordering regularizer while retaining outcome-reward fitting ( w/o ordering reg. ) lowers F1 and Hit@1 across all three datasets (Table 2 ). Absolute estimates reflect the accumulated KG search state, whereas differences between adjacent states estimate the change following each KG operation. Even with these changes retained, replacing multiplicative token weights with additive local advantages ( Additive local adv. ) causes the largest decrease among the variants, lowering CWQ F1 by 5.3 points. These results show that OACR improves final-answer quality by distinguishing KG operations while preserving the sign of the outcome-level advantage. sections.heading: Mismatch Analysis.
sections.text: Figure 4 compares the trajectory-to-operation mismatch rates of OACR and OACR GRPO across three datasets using Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-7B. OACR consistently achieves lower mismatch rates across all settings, with the largest reductions observed on CWQ: 6.7 and 5.8 percentage points for Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-7B, respectively. These results show that OACR mitigates the trajectory-to-operation mismatch that persists under outcome-only GRPO while improving final-answer quality.

sections.heading: Retrieval Coverage Analysis.
sections.text: We evaluate gold-answer retrieval before final-answer generation using Partial Coverage (PC) and Exact Coverage (EC), with definitions and full results in Appendix E . With Qwen2.5-3B, OACR achieves the highest PC and EC among the compared methods across all three datasets. On CWQ, PC and EC reach 90.1% and 87.9%. Their small gap indicates that most questions with at least one retrieved gold answer also have the complete gold answer set in their KG observations. Unlike F1 and Hit@1, these measures do not depend on the generated answer list. These results show that OACR retrieves complete gold answer sets for more questions, providing the entities needed for final-answer generation. Figure 5: Hyperparameter analysis on Qwen2.5-3B. sections.heading: Hyperparameter Sensitivity.
sections.text: Figure 5 shows the best overall performance at α = 0.3 \alpha=0.3 and c = 0.5 c=0.5 . Small α \alpha keeps token weights close to uniform, while small c c limits the contribution of estimated outcome-reward changes to operation credit. Larger values can give KG-operation tokens more weight at the expense of other policy-generated tokens. Removing temporal ordering regularization lowers performance, but emphasizing higher estimates at later states can conflict with outcome-reward fitting, potentially explaining the decline beyond η = 0.5 \eta=0.5 . Increasing λ \lambda weakens the reward for a correct first answer, consistent with lower Hit@1. F1 peaks at λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 , suggesting that this feedback helps predict the answer set. These results support OACR’s use of operation credit to improve final-answer quality through different token-level update magnitudes, rather than stronger reallocation or temporal ordering regularization.

sections.heading: Error Analysis.
sections.text: Figure 6 shows that Constraint Failure and Path Error account for 69.3% of the sampled OACR errors. Constraint Failure dominates CWQ, whereas Path Error is most frequent on WebQSP, indicating different difficulties in applying question constraints and selecting relations. In the Answer Mismatch case in Appendix J , the model retrieves the correct constellation but then expands to its member stars and returns them as answers. These failures suggest refining OACR’s operation credit for constraint application and relation selection, while improving the policy’s decision to end KG search once the required evidence has been retrieved as our future work.

sections.heading: Inference Efficiency Analysis.
sections.text: As detailed in Appendix D.1, on CWQ and WebQSP, OACR reduces output-token consumption by 32.3%–72.9% compared with KG-R1, ReknoS, and RoG in the reported same-backbone comparisons, while achieving higher Hit@1. This empirical analysis excludes EoG, DPRM, MCTS-KBQA, Graph-RFT, and SCPRM because we could not reproduce their results using the available implementations and settings. However, Appendix D.2 provides a qualitative comparison of their inference efficiency. To summarize, OACR combines shorter outputs with better final-answer quality in the reported comparisons, without invoking the KG-state outcome model during inference.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We identify a trajectory-to-operation mismatch in outcome-only GRPO for agentic KGQA: the rollout-level update direction can reinforce non-progressive entity-return operations and suppress progressive ones. OACR addresses this mismatch with a KG-state outcome model that converts estimated outcome-reward changes between adjacent KG search states into operation credit and positive token weights. These positive token weights rescale the outcome-level advantage at each policy-generated token while preserving its sign. Across three KGQA benchmarks, OACR consistently improves the SFT-initialized policy, increases gold-answer retrieval coverage, and reduces inference-time LLM calls and tokens. Future work will focus on maintaining question constraints across interaction turns and using failed rollouts to improve relation selection and relation direction.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: We identify two limitations of the current OACR design. First, the KG-state outcome model is periodically updated using a bounded rollout buffer. Its estimates may lag behind changes in the policy’s KG interactions between updates. Adapting the update frequency could account for these changes, but any improvement in estimation accuracy needs to be evaluated against the additional training cost. Second, OACR assigns one operation credit to each KG operation, so all tokens serializing that operation share the same weight. This does not separately weight entity and relation choices within an operation. Finer-grained weighting could distinguish these choices, but its benefit for final-answer quality remains to be evaluated.

sections.heading: LLM-based KGQA.
sections.text: Recent work uses LLMs to retrieve facts, plan relation paths, or constrain reasoning with KG structure. ToG ( Sun et al., 2024 ) performs training-free entity and relation expansion, while RoG ( Luo et al., 2024 ) generates relation paths for retrieving KG facts. PoG ( Chen et al., 2024 ) uses planning, memory, and reflection to revise KG search, and ReknoS ( Wang et al., 2025 ) uses super-relations to constrain KG reasoning. KBQA-o1 ( Luo et al., 2025 ) combines ReAct-style logical-form generation with Monte Carlo Tree Search for KG reasoning. RTSoG ( Long et al., 2025 ) uses reward-guided self-critic Monte Carlo Tree Search to retrieve and weight KG reasoning paths. SEAL ( Wang et al., 2026a ) uses agentic calibration, memory, and reflection to refine executable S-expressions for conversational KGQA. These methods improve KGQA through inference-time search, constrained decoding, or supervised trajectories, orthogonal to our OACR that directly optimizes a multi-turn KG interaction policy from sampled rollouts.

sections.heading: RL for agentic KGQA.
sections.text: Recent work optimizes KGQA agents from sampled rollouts. KG-R1 ( Song et al., 2025 ) formulates multi-turn KG interaction as a single-agent RL problem and optimizes the policy with outcome rewards. EoG ( Yan et al., 2026 ) combines outcome rewards with path-refined reward modeling to guide KG exploration. KnowCoder-A1 ( Chen et al., 2026b ) trains a ReAct-style KGQA agent through outcome-based rejection sampling and outcome-only curriculum RL. Graph-RFT ( Song et al., 2026 ) applies reinforcement fine-tuning to complex KG reasoning with adaptive KG and web retrieval. These methods optimize KGQA agents using rewards assigned to complete rollouts or paths. This provides limited distinction among KG operations within the same rollout, leaving the trajectory-to-operation mismatch unresolved. In contrast, our OACR converts estimated outcome-reward changes into operation credit to construct token weights for different KG operations.

sections.heading: Process rewards and credit assignment.
sections.text: Prior work assigns rewards or advantages to intermediate reasoning steps or interaction turns. PRMs score intermediate steps in multi-step LLM reasoning ( Lightman et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) , while methods for individual turns or steps estimate rewards or advantages during multi-turn agent interactions ( Zeng et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Rezaei et al., 2026 ) . Preference-based LLM optimization also assigns weights to training examples, text segments, or tokens ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Zeng et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . In KGQA, MCTS-KBQA ( Xiong et al., 2025 ) uses a step-wise reward mechanism to guide MCTS-based logical-form construction. DPRM ( Wang et al., 2026b ) trains separate PRMs for KG and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to derive step-level rewards from outcomes while modeling KG structural constraints and consistency between CoT reasoning and KG facts. SCPRM ( Chen et al., 2026a ) uses reasoning prefixes and schema distance to guide MCTS-based KG reasoning. These methods provide intermediate supervision, search guidance, or optimization weights. However, accumulated intermediate rewards or advantages can change the sign of the token-level advantage. In contrast, our OACR derives weights from outcome-reward changes between adjacent KG search states and preserves the sign of the outcome-level advantage.

sections.heading: Appendix B Dataset Statistics
sections.text: We evaluate OACR on three standard KGQA benchmarks, WebQSP ( Yih et al., 2016 ) , CWQ ( Talmor and Berant, 2018 ) , and GrailQA ( Gu et al., 2021 ) . We follow the commonly used evaluation split adopted in recent work ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Yan et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026b ) and report results on the test split. sections.heading: D.2 Qualitative Analysis
sections.text: For baselines excluded from the numerical comparison, we analyze the inference procedures described in their papers, separating candidate generation, candidate scoring, and retrieval. Candidate assessments are not equivalent to LLM calls, since multiple candidates may be processed together. This analysis identifies sources of inference-time computation without estimating unreported costs.

sections.heading: OACR.
sections.text: OACR generates KG operations and the final answer along a single interaction trajectory. The KG-state outcome model, operation-credit computation, and token reweighting are used only during training. Inference costs therefore arise from policy generation, KG-tool execution, and processing accumulated observations, without candidate scoring by Φ ϕ \Phi_{\phi} .

sections.heading: EoG.
sections.text: EoG ( Yan et al., 2026 ) uses outcome and path-refined rewards during RL, without a separate test-time reward evaluator in the described procedure. Its inference cost depends on processing the question and KG input and generating the reasoning and answer. The training reward design alone therefore does not establish an inference-cost difference from OACR.

sections.heading: DPRM.
sections.text: DPRM ( Wang et al., 2026b ) alternates KG-triple selection and CoT-step generation, using KG-PRM and CoT-PRM for Best-of- N N selection. Each iteration assesses N N KG candidates and N N CoT candidates, with N = 8 N=8 in the paper. Candidate generation and scoring therefore grow with both the number of iterations and N N , whereas OACR requires no inference-time PRM assessments or Best-of- N N selection.

sections.heading: MCTS-KBQA.
sections.text: MCTS-KBQA ( Xiong et al., 2025 ) expands multiple candidate actions and uses an instruction LLM to evaluate new intermediate states. Its computation includes branches outside the final selected path and depends on the expanded nodes, candidates per expansion, and evaluation-prompt lengths. The method bypasses terminal rollout simulation, so branching and intermediate-state evaluation are its main additional computations relative to OACR.

sections.heading: Graph-RFT.
sections.text: Graph-RFT ( Song et al., 2026 ) generates plans and interleaves reasoning with relation search, neighbor search, and Web search when KG information is insufficient. Its inference cost includes planning, tool invocations, and processing retrieved evidence. Web retrieval can add latency and input tokens but may also reduce unsuccessful KG exploration; training rewards do not constitute test-time scoring costs.

sections.heading: SCPRM.
sections.text: SCPRM ( Chen et al., 2026a ) evaluates candidate KG paths in SCPRM-MCTS using cumulative and schema-aware future rewards. Its scoring cost grows with the number and length of evaluated paths. The search returns endpoints of the highest-scoring paths rather than generating free-form answers, so output tokens alone omit reward-model evaluation during search. OACR does not require this inference-time path-scoring stage. OACR uses operation credit during training rather than candidate scoring during inference, avoiding the additional scoring computations of DPRM, MCTS-KBQA, and SCPRM. This distinction does not by itself determine latency, which also depends on generation, retrieval, and batching.

sections.heading: Appendix E Retrieval Coverage Analysis
sections.text: Figure 7 compares gold-answer retrieval coverage on CWQ, WebQSP, and GrailQA under the shared Qwen2.5-3B backbone. Partial Coverage (PC) is the percentage of questions for which at least one gold answer entity is returned during KG interaction, whereas Exact Coverage (EC) is the percentage for which the complete gold answer set is returned. OACR achieves the highest PC and EC on all three datasets. On CWQ, OACR reaches 90.1% PC and 87.9% EC, versus 55.9% and 44.1% for PoG. On WebQSP, OACR achieves 92.4% PC and 88.4% EC, exceeding the 77.5% PC of KG-R1 and the 62.5% EC of PoG. On GrailQA, OACR reaches 91.1% PC and 87.3% EC, versus 85.6% and 78.4% for PoG. Overall, OACR retrieves gold answer entities more reliably during KG interaction across all three datasets, showing that its improvement is not limited to final-answer generation. sections.heading: Appendix G State-Visit Statistics and Estimated Outcome-Reward Change Analysis
sections.text: We analyze repeated visits to the canonicalized question-state pairs used to train the KG-state outcome model. For each buffered rollout, every intermediate KG search state S t S_{t} contributes one visit to the corresponding question-state pair ( q , S t ) (q,S_{t}) , while the initial empty state S 0 S_{0} is excluded. Before aggregating visits, we canonicalize each question-state pair. For each relation-list operation, the action and entity fields are serialized in a fixed order. For each entity-return operation, the action , entity , and relation fields are serialized in a fixed order. Duplicate strings in each returned relation or entity list are removed, and the remaining strings are sorted lexicographically before the returned observation is serialized. The order of KG operations and returned observations across turns is preserved. Consequently, two question-state pairs are assigned the same aggregation key only when they contain the same question and the same ordered sequence of KG operations and canonicalized returned observations. This canonicalization removes differences caused only by field order, duplicate returned items, or the order of items within a returned list, without changing the KG search state across turns. The full canonicalized question-state pair is used as the aggregation key without observation truncation or lossy hashing. The 512-token maximum input length is applied only to the encoder input and does not affect target aggregation. Therefore, repeated question-state pairs in Table 8 correspond to exact canonical repeats under these rules rather than collisions caused by truncation or hashing. Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 arXiv:2610.25384v1 [cs.AI] 18 Oct 2026 Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation for Agentic Knowledge Graph Question Answering Mingyuan Li Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Novel Software Technology,Nanjing University, Nanjing, China Yucheng Li Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Novel Software Technology,Nanjing University, Nanjing, China Xiaxia Wang Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of Oxford * Corresponding author: gcheng@nju.edu.cn Gong Cheng Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Novel Software Technology,Nanjing University, Nanjing, China Abstract Agentic knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) requires large language models (LLMs) to solve complex questions through multi-turn interactions with a knowledge graph (KG). Outcome-supervised reinforcement learning derives verifiable outcome rewards from final answers but uniformly assigns each rollout’s outcome-level advantage to all policy-generated tokens, creating a trajectory-to-operation mismatch since KG operations within a rollout can have varying effects on the search process and final answer. To address this, we propose Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation (OACR), which employs a training-only KG-state outcome model to estimate outcome-reward changes between adjacent KG search states and converts them into operation credit, from which token-wise weights are derived. These multiplicative weights reallocate token-level update magnitudes while preserving the sign of the outcome-level advantage at every generated token. Across three benchmarks, OACR achieves stronger overall performance than existing KGQA methods while using fewer inference-time LLM calls and tokens. A Preprint 1 Introduction Figure 1: Trajectory-to-operation mismatch under outcome-supervised RL. Left: Successful rollouts may contain non-progressive entity-return operations, while failed rollouts may contain progressive ones. Right: Distribution of progressive and non-progressive entity-return operations across successful and failed rollouts, based on 5,000 such operations generated by Qwen2.5-3B on CWQ. Knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) seeks to answer natural language questions by reasoning over facts represented as directed triples in a knowledge graph (KG) ( Ma et al., 2025 ; Nguyen et al., 2025 ; Tian et al., 2025 ) . Complex KGQA often requires multi-hop reasoning: a model must select relation paths that reach answer entities, follow the correct directions, and avoid irrelevant branches ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Ao et al., 2025 ) . Recent agentic methods based on large language models (LLMs) formulate KGQA as multi-turn interaction with a KG environment ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2024 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Yan et al., 2026 ) . At each turn, the agent issues a schema-valid KG operation, receives a structured observation containing returned relations or entities, and appends both to the accumulated KG search state. This interaction process is well suited to outcome-supervised reinforcement learning (RL): final answers provide verifiable outcome rewards, whereas labels that directly assess the utility of individual KG operations are costly to obtain and usually unavailable during training. We label an entity-return operation as progressive if it reduces the minimum shortest-path distance between the accumulated entity set and the gold answer set, and non-progressive otherwise. Retrieving additional gold answers or verifying constraints may leave this distance unchanged. Figure 2: Training-process diagnostics of outcome-only GRPO in agentic KGQA. (a) Final-answer quality. (b) Raw and smoothed trajectory-to-operation mismatch rates. (c) Rates of rollouts containing both progressive and non-progressive entity-return operations and of non-progressive operations following the first progressive one. (d) Average numbers of all KG operations and entity-return operations per rollout. Motivation. Figure 1 summarizes 5,000 entity-return operations from rollouts generated on ComplexWebQuestions (CWQ) ( Talmor and Berant, 2018 ) by a Qwen2.5-3B model trained with outcome-only Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . In successful rollouts, 65.8% of entity-return operations are non-progressive, while 25.3% in failed rollouts are progressive. Thus, rollout outcome cannot determine whether individual entity-return operations advance KG search. Nevertheless, outcome-supervised RL assigns the same outcome-level advantage to all policy-generated tokens in a rollout, including those serializing progressive and non-progressive operations. We call this mismatch between rollout-level supervision and individual KG-operation effects trajectory-to-operation mismatch . We further examine whether outcome-only GRPO reduces this mismatch. Figure 2 reports the training-process diagnostics. Panel (a) shows both F1 and Hit@1 rising during training, whereas Panel (b) shows the mismatch rate fluctuating between 33% and 36%. Here, a mismatch is a non-progressive entity-return operation in a successful rollout or a progressive operation in a failed rollout. Panel (c) shows that the rate of rollouts containing both progressive and non-progressive entity-return operations remains at 36% to 40%, while the rate of non-progressive entity-return operations after the first progressive operation fluctuates between 42% and 68% and increases toward the end of training. Panel (d) shows that the average interaction length remains stable at 2.9 KG operations and 1.45 entity-return operations per rollout. Together, Figures 1 and 2 show that outcome-only GRPO improves final-answer performance, yet the trajectory-to-operation mismatch persists throughout training and is not explained by changes in KG interaction length. These observations necessitate a credit-assignment method that distinguishes KG operations within a rollout while preserving the sign of outcome-level advantage. A common alternative uses Process Reward Models (PRMs) to score intermediate steps ( Lightman et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) . However, an operation’s effect on the outcome reward depends on subsequent operations and final-answer generation, so treating these scores as independent local rewards or additive local advantages can adversely change the sign of the token-level advantage. Our Work. We propose Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation (OACR) for outcome-supervised agentic KGQA. OACR computes an outcome-level advantage from the rewards of rollouts sampled for the same question and incorporates a KG-state outcome model to estimate outcome-reward changes between adjacent KG search states. It converts these changes into operation credit, assigning larger weights to tokens that serialize KG operations assigned greater credit. The token weights are normalized over all policy-generated tokens in the rollout and remain positive. Multiplying these positive weights by the outcome-level advantage reallocates its magnitude across policy-generated tokens while preserving its sign. The KG-state outcome model is used only during training and introduces no additional inference-time cost. Across three benchmarks, OACR outperforms existing KGQA methods overall while using fewer inference-time LLM calls and tokens. Our main contributions are as follows. • We identify and empirically analyze trajectory-to-operation mismatch under outcome-supervised RL for agentic KGQA: the final-answer outcome does not distinguish whether individual KG operations advance KG search, yet all policy-generated tokens within a rollout receive the same outcome-level advantage. This mismatch persists throughout training. • We propose OACR, which converts estimated outcome-reward changes between adjacent KG search states into operation credit used to construct token weights, thereby reallocating token-level update magnitudes while preserving the sign of the outcome-level advantage. Our code is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/OACR/. 2 Related Work Further discussion of these related methods is provided in Appendix A . LLM-based KGQA. LLM-based KGQA formulates reasoning as explicit KG search, enabling LLMs to construct or revise search decisions for retrieving KG facts ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Long et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . These methods improve KGQA through inference-time search, constrained decoding, or supervised trajectories, orthogonal to our OACR that optimizes a multi-turn KG interaction policy from sampled rollouts. RL for agentic KGQA. Recent work trains KGQA agents from sampled rollouts using outcome rewards or reinforcement fine-tuning to optimize multi-turn KG interaction policies ( Song et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2026 ) . Other studies refine outcome supervision through reward modeling, rejection sampling, or curriculum RL ( Yan et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026b ) . These methods assign rewards to complete rollouts or paths, providing limited distinction among KG operations within a rollout and leaving the trajectory-to-operation mismatch unresolved. In contrast, OACR converts estimated outcome-reward changes into operation credit for constructing token weights across KG operations. Process rewards and credit assignment. Prior work assigns rewards or advantages to intermediate reasoning steps or interaction turns, while preference-based optimization reweights training examples, text segments, or tokens ( Lightman et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ; Zeng et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Rezaei et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Zeng et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . In KGQA, related approaches use step-wise rewards, process reward models, or KG schema information to guide logical-form construction and KG reasoning ( Xiong et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Chen et al., 2026a ) . These methods provide intermediate supervision, search guidance, or optimization weights. However, accumulated intermediate rewards or advantages can change the sign of the token-level advantage. In contrast, our OACR derives weights from outcome-reward changes between adjacent KG search states and preserves the sign of the outcome-level advantage. Figure 3: Overview of OACR. Supervised fine-tuning initializes a KGQA agent, followed by outcome-supervised reinforcement learning with outcome-anchored credit reallocation. The KG-state outcome model is updated using recent OACR rollouts every U U RL iterations and held fixed during each policy update. The entire process is outlined in Algorithm 2 of Appendix F . 3 Method Figure 3 presents the two-stage OACR pipeline. Stage 1 uses supervised fine-tuning to initialize the KGQA policy. In Stage 2, the current policy samples rollout groups and computes an outcome-level advantage for each rollout. The KG-state outcome model is initially trained on outcome-only GRPO rollouts and periodically updated using recent OACR rollouts. Its estimates for adjacent KG search states are used to compute operation credit and construct token weights. These weights rescale the outcome-level advantage across policy-generated tokens while preserving its sign. To summarize, OACR combines shorter outputs with better final-answer quality in the reported comparisons, without invoking the KG-state outcome model during inference. 5 Conclusion We identify a trajectory-to-operation mismatch in outcome-only GRPO for agentic KGQA: the rollout-level update direction can reinforce non-progressive entity-return operations and suppress progressive ones. OACR addresses this mismatch with a KG-state outcome model that converts estimated outcome-reward changes between adjacent KG search states into operation credit and positive token weights. These positive token weights rescale the outcome-level advantage at each policy-generated token while preserving its sign. Across three KGQA benchmarks, OACR consistently improves the SFT-initialized policy, increases gold-answer retrieval coverage, and reduces inference-time LLM calls and tokens. Future work will focus on maintaining question constraints across interaction turns and using failed rollouts to improve relation selection and relation direction. Limitations We identify two limitations of the current OACR design. First, the KG-state outcome model is periodically updated using a bounded rollout buffer. Its estimates may lag behind changes in the policy’s KG interactions between updates. Adapting the update frequency could account for these changes, but any improvement in estimation accuracy needs to be evaluated against the additional training cost. Second, OACR assigns one operation credit to each KG operation, so all tokens serializing that operation share the same weight. Recent work uses LLMs to retrieve facts, plan relation paths, or constrain reasoning with KG structure. ToG ( Sun et al., 2024 ) performs training-free entity and relation expansion, while RoG ( Luo et al., 2024 ) generates relation paths for retrieving KG facts. PoG ( Chen et al., 2024 ) uses planning, memory, and reflection to revise KG search, and ReknoS ( Wang et al., 2025 ) uses super-relations to constrain KG reasoning. KBQA-o1 ( Luo et al., 2025 ) combines ReAct-style logical-form generation with Monte Carlo Tree Search for KG reasoning. RTSoG ( Long et al., 2025 ) uses reward-guided self-critic Monte Carlo Tree Search to retrieve and weight KG reasoning paths. SEAL ( Wang et al., 2026a ) uses agentic calibration, memory, and reflection to refine executable S-expressions for conversational KGQA. These methods improve KGQA through inference-time search, constrained decoding, or supervised trajectories, orthogonal to our OACR that directly optimizes a multi-turn KG interaction policy from sampled rollouts. RL for agentic KGQA. Recent work optimizes KGQA agents from sampled rollouts. KG-R1 ( Song et al., 2025 ) formulates multi-turn KG interaction as a single-agent RL problem and optimizes the policy with outcome rewards. EoG ( Yan et al., 2026 ) combines outcome rewards with path-refined reward modeling to guide KG exploration. KnowCoder-A1 ( Chen et al., 2026b ) trains a ReAct-style KGQA agent through outcome-based rejection sampling and outcome-only curriculum RL. Graph-RFT ( Song et al., 2026 ) applies reinforcement fine-tuning to complex KG reasoning with adaptive KG and web retrieval. These methods optimize KGQA agents using rewards assigned to complete rollouts or paths. This provides limited distinction among KG operations within the same rollout, leaving the trajectory-to-operation mismatch unresolved. In contrast, our OACR converts estimated outcome-reward changes into operation credit to construct token weights for different KG operations. Process rewards and credit assignment. Prior work assigns rewards or advantages to intermediate reasoning steps or interaction turns. PRMs score intermediate steps in multi-step LLM reasoning ( Lightman et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) , while methods for individual turns or steps estimate rewards or advantages during multi-turn agent interactions ( Zeng et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Rezaei et al., 2026 ) . Preference-based LLM optimization also assigns weights to training examples, text segments, or tokens ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Zeng et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . In KGQA, MCTS-KBQA ( Xiong et al., 2025 ) uses a step-wise reward mechanism to guide MCTS-based logical-form construction. DPRM ( Wang et al., 2026b ) trains separate PRMs for KG and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to derive step-level rewards from outcomes while modeling KG structural constraints and consistency between CoT reasoning and KG facts. SCPRM ( Chen et al., 2026a ) uses reasoning prefixes and schema distance to guide MCTS-based KG reasoning. These methods provide intermediate supervision, search guidance, or optimization weights. However, accumulated intermediate rewards or advantages can change the sign of the token-level advantage. In contrast, our OACR derives weights from outcome-reward changes between adjacent KG search states and preserves the sign of the outcome-level advantage. D.2 Qualitative Analysis For baselines excluded from the numerical comparison, we analyze the inference procedures described in their papers, separating candidate generation, candidate scoring, and retrieval. Candidate assessments are not equivalent to LLM calls, since multiple candidates may be processed together. This analysis identifies sources of inference-time computation without estimating unreported costs. OACR. OACR generates KG operations and the final answer along a single interaction trajectory. The KG-state outcome model, operation-credit computation, and token reweighting are used only during training. Inference costs therefore arise from policy generation, KG-tool execution, and processing accumulated observations, without candidate scoring by Φ ϕ \Phi_{\phi} . EoG. EoG ( Yan et al., 2026 ) uses outcome and path-refined rewards during RL, without a separate test-time reward evaluator in the described procedure. Its inference cost depends on processing the question and KG input and generating the reasoning and answer. The training reward design alone therefore does not establish an inference-cost difference from OACR. DPRM. DPRM ( Wang et al., 2026b ) alternates KG-triple selection and CoT-step generation, using KG-PRM and CoT-PRM for Best-of- N N selection. Each iteration assesses N N KG candidates and N N CoT candidates, with N = 8 N=8 in the paper. Candidate generation and scoring therefore grow with both the number of iterations and N N , whereas OACR requires no inference-time PRM assessments or Best-of- N N selection. MCTS-KBQA. MCTS-KBQA ( Xiong et al., 2025 ) expands multiple candidate actions and uses an instruction LLM to evaluate new intermediate states. Its computation includes branches outside the final selected path and depends on the expanded nodes, candidates per expansion, and evaluation-prompt lengths. The method bypasses terminal rollout simulation, so branching and intermediate-state evaluation are its main additional computations relative to OACR. Graph-RFT. Graph-RFT ( Song et al., 2026 ) generates plans and interleaves reasoning with relation search, neighbor search, and Web search when KG information is insufficient. Its inference cost includes planning, tool invocations, and processing retrieved evidence. Web retrieval can add latency and input tokens but may also reduce unsuccessful KG exploration; training rewards do not constitute test-time scoring costs. SCPRM. SCPRM ( Chen et al., 2026a ) evaluates candidate KG paths in SCPRM-MCTS using cumulative and schema-aware future rewards. Its scoring cost grows with the number and length of evaluated paths. The search returns endpoints of the highest-scoring paths rather than generating free-form answers, so output tokens alone omit reward-model evaluation during search. OACR does not require this inference-time path-scoring stage. OACR uses operation credit during training rather than candidate scoring during inference, avoiding the additional scoring computations of DPRM, MCTS-KBQA, and SCPRM. This distinction does not by itself determine latency, which also depends on generation, retrieval, and batching. Before aggregating visits, we canonicalize each question-state pair. For each relation-list operation, the action and entity fields are serialized in a fixed order. For each entity-return operation, the action , entity , and relation fields are serialized in a fixed order. Duplicate strings in each returned relation or entity list are removed, and the remaining strings are sorted lexicographically before the returned observation is serialized. The order of KG operations and returned observations across turns is preserved. Consequently, two question-state pairs are assigned the same aggregation key only when they contain the same question and the same ordered sequence of KG operations and canonicalized returned observations. This canonicalization removes differences caused only by field order, duplicate returned items, or the order of items within a returned list, without changing the KG search state across turns. The full canonicalized question-state pair is used as the aggregation key without observation truncation or lossy hashing. The 512-token maximum input length is applied only to the encoder input and does not affect target aggregation.
